_description:
# Help and flag placement

Where flags may go, which commands differ, help levels and short names.
placement:
# A flag goes after its level

A command has levels: the program, its subcommand, the action (`aos-agent`, `ctl`, `stop`). A flag belongs to one level and may go anywhere after that level's name, also after later names and arguments. These are the same:

```sh
aos-agent -d /srv/d ctl stop bob
aos-agent ctl stop bob -d /srv/d
aos-agent ctl stop -t bob
aos-tools add tools/clock --name now
```

This holds for every aos command, the parts in `aos/cli/parts/` too (`aos-json get FILE#/a --str`, `aos-eca-turn /abs/def --one`). Exceptions, where words are handed on as they are: everything after the folder in `aos-exec FOLDER ARGS` goes to that folder's program; `aos-sandbox CONFIG PROG ...` hands PROG and its args on;`aos-mcp-launch SERVER_FILE` takes no flags; `aos-json set`, `append` and `merge` take their flags before FILE, because the value may be any word (`aos-json set --str FILE#/a -x`). A word after an argument that looks like a negative number (`-3`) or holds a space stays an argument.
target:
# Naming the agent in aos-agent

`aos-agent ctl` start / stop / sleep / wake / pause / resume / where take the agent as `-t NAME` or as the last argument. say, listen, chat, open, close, watch, tools, llm, system, history, hook, goal and `ctl state` take only `-t` (state's other words are part names). `ctl add / rm / set-def / ls / who` take no `-t`. Two different names = `ArgumentsBad`.

No `-t` and no `$AOS_AGENT` (empty counts as not set): aos-agent looks in the current folder, `./.stack` first, then `./`. A folder counts only if it has `stderr.txt` (the daemon writes it in the stack of every proc it starts) and its real path is the `stack` of a row on the daemon's table; that row's name is the target. `./.stack` missing or without `stderr.txt` (such as a tree root, where `.stack` is the daemon's own) = try `./`. Has `stderr.txt` but is on no row = `InstanceMissing`. Neither = `TargetMissing`. Only the stack folder itself counts, not a folder inside it, and never a definition folder. No `-d` and no `$AOS_DAEMON` either: the daemon is two folders up from that stack (the default layout `<daemon stack>/procs/NAME`); that folder must have `procs_state.json` and list the stack, else `DaemonMissing`. This holds with `-t` too (inside ann's stack, `-t bob` is bob on the same daemon). A stack attached elsewhere with `-s` needs `-d`. The tree root's `./.stack` is never taken as the daemon. This is a shortcut for people who know the folder is an agent's stack; nothing in the stack says which daemon it belongs to.

```sh
cd /abs/tree/.stack/procs/ann && aos-agent say hello   # target = ann, daemon = /abs/tree/.stack
```
text:
# Text ends flag reading

Text that is handed on as it is ends flag reading: everything from the first word of `aos-agent say WORDS`, `history summarize RANGE TEXT` (or `summarize -n K TEXT`), `history set LINE JSON`, `goal set TEXT`, `aos-mailbox send WHAT`, `aos-clock-register add NAME TEXT` is text, so put flags before it. After `--` nothing is a flag: `aos-daemon-ctl add tools/job -- --verbose`, `aos-agent say -t bob -- -hello`.
help:
# Help levels

Run `aos-agent --help`, then `aos-agent tools --help`, then `aos-agent tools add --help`. Each prints only its own level. Help needs no live daemon or target. Commands with subcommands work the same: `aos-post send --help`, `aos-json set --help`.

A flag nobody in the command knows gives `FlagUnknown`. No subcommand gives `ArgumentsBad` (`aos-post: error: ArgumentsBad missing subcommand`); an unknown subcommand gives `CommandUnknown`.
short:
# Short names

Common default short names are: `-h --help`, `-d --daemon`, `-t --target`, `-j --json`, `-n --name`, `-w --ws`, `-s --stack`, `-f --follow`, `-y --yes`. Each command defines its own short names and may give them different meanings (aos-mailbox `-s` is your own stack; aos-clock-register `-c` is the clock). Only use a short name where that help lists it. `--file`, `--detach` and `--timeout-s` have no short name. `-s`/`-w` are not aliases for the switches in `ctl where`, or the path in `ctl who`.

Use separate tokens: `-t bob`. `-tbob` and `-jf` are unknown flags.
